title: Gaussian particles without gradients
one_liner: To find good probability distributions without computing gradients, release a swarm of Gaussian particles that bounce around and agree on where the answer is.
lead: Variational inference (the task of finding a simple bell curve that matches a messy, complicated target distribution — the pattern of how likely each outcome is) is hard because the standard toolbox uses gradients (which direction to nudge numbers downhill), and those are expensive and fragile when the target is bumpy and lopsided. This paper proposes a zeroth-order method — it uses no gradients at all — by deploying a swarm of Gaussian particles that explore the space, find where the good answers cluster, and self-organize around global minima through a consensus mechanism.

problem.h2: Finding probability distributions is tricky without gradients
paras: Variational inference asks: given a messy, hard-to-work-with target distribution (think of the log-probability surface as having many peaks and valleys), find a simpler one — usually a bell curve (Gaussian) — that sits on top of it. The two should overlap as much as possible.

The standard approach computes gradients (which direction to nudge the bell curve's parameters to improve the overlap). But when the target has lopsided peaks (meaning the peaks are not symmetric bell shapes), gradients can be unreliable: they point you downhill locally, but you miss the true global peak because the terrain is deceptive. Also, computing those gradients is expensive.
A naive first attempt: pick random bell curves and score each one. Keep the best and move slightly toward it. But random search is wasteful — you waste effort on obviously bad parts of the space.

callout.html: The paper uses a swarm of Gaussian particles that explore without gradients, finding consensus around the best answers.

steps.text: Initialize a swarm of Gaussian distributions spread across the search space.
Each particle randomally (randomly) moves around, sampling its own uncertainty.
Evaluate each particle's location against the target distribution. No gradients needed, only scores.
Each particle pulls toward the weighted average of all particles, biased toward higher-scoring ones.
The swarm self-organizes into a tight cluster centered on the global optimum.

paras: The core move is the introduction of the Linearized Bures-Wasserstein (LBW) space, a new way to write down Gaussian bell curves. Instead of describing a Gaussian the usual way (with parameters that live in regular flat space), the LBW space changes the coordinate system so that 'moving toward agreement' between particles becomes shorter and more direct. This makes the consensus-based exploration more efficient, because in LBW space a unit step in parameter space corresponds to a smaller distortion of the Gaussian shape, so particles waste less energy on irrelevant parameter jiggling and converge faster to the true answer.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: particle consensus strength
hidden.name: How tightly the swarm agrees
paras: The paper does not give it an explicit name, but the engine is a hidden quantity: how much each particle is pulled toward the center of mass (weighted by scores). In consensus-based optimization, stronger agreement pulls particles tighter together because each particle is more influenced by what the others are doing, so they form a cohesive group instead of a scattered cloud; weaker agreement lets them explore more because each particle mostly ignores the others and continues its own random walk.

The paper measures this implicitly through the mean-field approximation, a mathematical model that treats the entire swarm as a smooth distribution rather than discrete particles. By studying how this smooth distribution evolves over time, they verify that particles do converge to the global minimum because the mathematics shows that consensus weight, combined with random exploration, drives the swarm's center toward lower and lower error values.

heat.caption: Darker means stronger pull toward consensus. Stronger agreement at high-scoring regions (marked).

reads.html: Consensus strength is simply how much each particle listens to the average position of the others. Strong consensus means tight coordination; weak means more independent exploration.
The paper analyzes consensus weight through the mean-field limit, showing that particles asymptotically concentrate at global minima of the target distribution.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: exploration meets agreement
paras: The mechanism has two parts. First, each particle explores randomly (stochastically moves) so that the swarm collectively samples many regions of the space and does not get trapped in a single local valley. Second, each particle also pulls toward the weighted average of all other particles, with weights proportional to how good each particle is (its score). This creates a feedback loop: particles that land in good regions attract others, so more particles cluster there, making that region pull even harder. Over time, the swarm self-organizes and concentrates on the globally best region without any particle ever computing a gradient.

The LBW parametrization makes this consensus mechanism work smoothly. In the standard parametrization, pulling two Gaussians toward agreement can involve awkward warping and distortions. In LBW space, agreement is more direct and efficient — less energy is wasted on unproductive parameter changes. This is why the paper introduces it as the foundation of the algorithm.

stages.s: Target distribution (the messy one we want to match)
Each particle explores via random walk
Consensus pulls toward high-scoring neighbors in LBW space
Swarm converges to Gaussian matching the target

math.words: Each particle moves in two ways: a random kick (exploration) plus a pull toward the weighted average of all particles (consensus), where the weights are determined by how well each particle scores against the target.
math.equation: dX_i = sqrt(2) dW_i + lambda * sum_j w_j (X_j - X_i) dt
symbols: position of particle i in LBW space
strength of consensus pulling (how much particles listen to neighbors)
weight of particle j, based on its score (higher score, more influence)
direction to particle j; pulling makes particles cluster

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose we have 3 particles at positions 10, 15, and 20 (in LBW space).
Particle 1 at position 10 has score 0.3; Particle 2 at 15 has score 0.7; Particle 3 at 20 has score 0.5.
Particle 1 pulls from 10 toward 16.15 (away from worse neighbors, toward better ones).
Particle 3 pulls from 20 toward 16.15 (the high-scoring region pulls everything together).
With strong lambda, particles converge; with weak lambda, they explore longer before agreeing.

math.note: The random noise lets particles escape local traps; consensus weights steer them toward the global best region, where many particles already sit.

charts.title: Gradient-based method (standard)
charts.note: Gradients climb the nearest local peak; on targets with multiple peaks, you often get stuck at the wrong one.

charts.title: This paper (particle swarm)
charts.note: The swarm collectively finds the global peak even on non-log-concave targets because particles share information.

items.html: If lambda is too low, particles keep exploring forever and never commit to an answer. You need enough agreement weight to actually converge.

items.b: High-dimensional space still means many particles needed.
items.html: To explore all regions thoroughly, you may need hundreds or thousands of particles. Each particle is a Gaussian, so memory and compute scale with swarm size, especially in very high dimensions.

items.b: Scoring each particle is the bottleneck.
items.html: Even without gradients, you still must evaluate the target distribution at each particle's location. If that evaluation is expensive, the swarm approach gains less advantage over gradient methods.

items.b: Works well when target is non-log-concave.
items.html: The paper shines on bumpy, lopsided targets where gradients fail because each particle can explore independently and share information to escape local traps. On smooth, bowl-shaped targets, gradient methods may be faster because there are no local traps to escape — a single gradient step marches directly toward the global answer.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple non-log-concave target: a mixture of two distant Gaussians (two sharp peaks far apart) or a U-shaped valley with steep sides. Initialize a particle swarm and a gradient-based optimizer at the same random starting point. Run both for the same budget of target evaluations. The particle swarm should find the true global mixture; the gradient method should get stuck in one peak.
demo.metric_eq: Accuracy = how close the swarm's converged Gaussian is to the true target (measured by Wasserstein distance)
demo.closing: The demo proves that on non-log-concave targets, a swarm that shares information globally outperforms a single optimizer that only follows local gradients because the swarm's diversity allows it to sample multiple peaks in parallel and then coordinate on the tallest one, while a single gradient optimizer simply climbs whichever peak it started nearest to.
